lead: A voltage-to-current converter turns an input voltage into a current that the load cannot change. The op-amp holds a fixed voltage across a resistor R, so Ohm's law fixes the current through R, and that same current must flow through the load. The reverse circuit, the current-to-voltage converter, pins its input at zero volts and turns an input current into a proportional output voltage. Both sit inside LED drivers, 4–20 mA transmitters, photodiode receivers and DAC output stages, wherever current is the quantity that matters.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for the virtual short and saturation, Chapter 6.2 for the inverting configuration, and Ohm's law.

sections.h3: Floating load: current set by R

blocks.text: Many loads want a set current, not a set voltage. An LED's brightness, the pull of a coil and the signal in a 4–20 mA loop all follow current. Drive them from a voltage divider and the current changes the moment the load resistance changes. A voltage-to-current converter removes that dependence.

Connect the input voltage v<sub>in</sub> to the non-inverting input. Put resistor R from the inverting input to ground. Put the load R<sub>L</sub> from the op-amp output back to the inverting input. The load floats: neither of its ends is at ground.

Negative feedback gives a virtual short, so the inverting input sits at vin (see Chapter 6.1). The op-amp inputs draw no current, so every ampere that flows through R must arrive through the load. The voltage across R is vin, so the load current is vin/R.

blocks.where: v<sub>in</sub> is the input voltage in volts (V), R is the sense resistor in ohms (Ω), and I<sub>L</sub> is the load current in amperes (A).

blocks.text: The current depends on v<sub>in</sub> and R alone. Change R<sub>L</sub> and the op-amp moves its output instead: v<sub>out</sub> = v<sub>in</sub> + I<sub>L</sub>R<sub>L</sub> = v<sub>in</sub>(1 + R<sub>L</sub>/R). The bottom of the load rides at v<sub>in</sub>, which is why it must float. LED and laser diode drivers use this circuit directly, because light output follows current.

sections.h3: Grounded load: the Howland current pump

blocks.text: A floating load is awkward. Many sensors and LEDs need one end at ground. The Howland current pump drives a grounded load. It places the sense resistor R in series with the load and compares the drop across R with v<sub>in</sub>, using a bridge of four resistors R1 to R4. When the bridge ratios match, R1/R2 = R3/R4, the op-amp drives its output until that drop equals v<sub>in</sub>.
The load current is again v<sub>in</sub>/R, and the output is v<sub>in</sub> plus the load voltage. Raise R<sub>L</sub> and the output rises; the current stays.
I<sub>L</sub> = v<sub>in</sub> / R,   v<sub>out</sub> = v<sub>in</sub> + I<sub>L</sub>R<sub>L</sub>
blocks.where: R is the sense resistor (Ω), R<sub>L</sub> the grounded load (Ω), v<sub>out</sub> the op-amp output (V). Matched ratios R1/R2 = R3/R4 keep I<sub>L</sub> free of R<sub>L</sub>.

blocks.text: Matching matters. A 1 % error in one resistor makes part of the output current follow the load voltage, so I<sub>L</sub> drifts as R<sub>L</sub> changes. Use a matched resistor array or trim one resistor.

The op-amp output cannot pass its saturation level V<sub>sat</sub>, about the supply rail minus 1 V to 2 V. The largest load it can drive is (V<sub>sat</sub> − v<sub>in</sub>)/I<sub>L</sub>. Past that value the op-amp saturates, the drop across R falls below v<sub>in</sub> and the current collapses. This allowed load range is the compliance of the source.

blocks.where: V<sub>sat</sub> is the saturation output, close to the supply rail (V); I<sub>L</sub> = v<sub>in</sub>/R (A); R<sub>L(max)</sub> in ohms (Ω).

sections.h3: Current to voltage: the transimpedance amplifier

blocks.text: Some sources deliver a current: a photodiode, a current-output DAC, a 4–20 mA receiver. Passing that current through a resistor to ground gives a voltage, but the source then sees a voltage that swings with its own current. A photodiode's capacitance must charge and discharge through that swing, which slows the circuit.

The transimpedance amplifier holds the source node still. The current I<sub>in</sub> enters the inverting input, R<sub>f</sub> goes from the output to that input, and the non-inverting input is grounded. The virtual short pins the inverting node at 0 V, so the input resistance is close to zero and all of I<sub>in</sub> flows in R<sub>f</sub>.

blocks.where: I<sub>in</sub> is the input current in amperes (A), R<sub>f</sub> the feedback resistor in ohms (Ω), v<sub>out</sub> in volts (V). Input resistance ≈ 0 Ω because the node is a virtual ground.

blocks.text: The minus sign says the output falls when current is pushed into the node. A photodiode delivering 10 µA through R<sub>f</sub> = 100 kΩ gives −1 V, and its own capacitance never charges because its terminal stays at 0 V. That is why this front end is fast.

Source capacitance C<sub>s</sub> and R<sub>f</sub> form a pole that can peak the response and even oscillate. Add C<sub>f</sub> across R<sub>f</sub>. Its pole at 1/(2πR<sub>f</sub>C<sub>f</sub>) rolls off the loop gain before the crossing and trades bandwidth for a clean output. Too small a C<sub>f</sub> rings; too large slows the receiver.

items: LED and laser diode drivers: current sets light output, and the diode is protected from overcurrent.
4–20 mA transmitters: a sensor voltage becomes a loop current that survives long cables and voltage drops.
Photodiode front ends: the transimpedance stage turns microamps of light current into volts for an ADC.
DAC outputs: a current-steering DAC feeds a transimpedance stage to give a clean voltage.

figure.caption: The op-amp holds the drop across R equal to v_in, so the current into the load is set by R and v_in alone. Change the load and the output voltage moves, not the current.

spec.title: Voltage-to-current converter
spec.aria: Voltage-to-current conversion: the op-amp keeps the voltage across R equal to v_in, so the current pushed into the load is v_in divided by R.

examples.question: A Howland current pump uses R = 1 kΩ with v_in = 2 V to drive a grounded load R_L = 500 Ω. The op-amp runs on ±12 V supplies and saturates at 12 V. (a) Find the load current and the load voltage. (b) Find the op-amp output voltage and check it against the rails. (c) Find the largest load resistance for which the circuit still acts as a current source. (d) A photodiode sends 10 µA into a transimpedance amplifier with R_f = 100 kΩ; find v_out.
steps: The bridge is matched, so the drop across R is held at v_in = 2 V.
I_L = v_in/R = 2 V / 1 kΩ = 2 mA. This value does not contain R_L.
V_L = I_L R_L = 2 mA × 500 Ω = 1 V.
v_out = v_in + V_L = 3 V. The rails are ±12 V, so 3 V is well inside them and the op-amp can source 2 mA.
At the compliance limit v_out = V_sat = 12 V, so R_L(max) = (12 V − 2 V) / 2 mA = 5 kΩ.
Transimpedance stage: v_out = −I_in R_f = −(10 µA)(100 kΩ) = −1 V.
examples.answer: The load current is 2 mA, the load voltage 1 V, the op-amp output 3 V, the largest load resistance 5 kΩ, and the photodiode output −1 V.
examples.check:
R = 1e3
vin = 2.0
RL = 500.0
Vsat = 12.0
I = vin / R
VL = I * RL
vout = vin + VL
RLmax = (Vsat - vin) / I
Iph = 10e-6
Rf = 100e3
vout_ph = -Iph * Rf
print(I)
print(VL)
print(vout)
print(RLmax)
print(vout_ph)

traps: Assuming the current holds for any load. Past the compliance limit the op-amp saturates and the current collapses; always check that v_in + I_L R_L is inside the rails.
Using V_sat/I_L as the largest load. The sense resistor takes v_in first, so R_L(max) = (V_sat − v_in)/I_L, a smaller value.
Mismatched Howland resistors. With R1/R2 ≠ R3/R4 part of the output current follows the load voltage, so the circuit is no longer a current source.
Calling the transimpedance input resistance R_f. It is near zero, because the input node is a virtual ground.
Sign and unit slips: v_out = −I_in R_f, and 10 µA × 100 kΩ = 1 V. Watch µA against kΩ and mA against kΩ.

quiz.q: In the floating-load voltage-to-current converter, what sets the load current?
quiz.a: The input voltage v_in and the sense resistor R: I_L = v_in/R. The load resistance does not appear.

quiz.q: Why does the load current stay the same when the load resistance changes?
quiz.a: The op-amp keeps v_in across R, so the current in R is fixed. That same current must flow through the load, so the op-amp changes v_out instead.

quiz.q: A floating-load converter has R = 2 kΩ, v_in = 1.5 V, R_L = 1 kΩ, ±15 V supplies and saturation at 15 V. Find I_L, V_L, v_out and R_L(max).
A Howland pump has R1 = R2 = 10 kΩ but R3 = 9 kΩ and R4 = 10 kΩ. What happens to the load current as R_L changes?
quiz.a: The bridge is unbalanced, so the output current gains a term proportional to the load voltage. I_L then depends on R_L and the circuit behaves partly as a voltage source.

quiz.q: A photodiode gives 25 µA into a transimpedance amplifier with R_f = 47 kΩ. Find v_out.
Why is C_f added across R_f in a transimpedance amplifier?
quiz.a: Source capacitance with R_f makes a pole that peaks the response or oscillates. C_f adds a feedback pole that rolls off the loop gain first, trading bandwidth for stability.

quiz.q: With ±12 V supplies, v_in = 2 V and R = 1 kΩ, the current is 2 mA up to R_L = 5 kΩ. What happens at R_L = 8 kΩ, and why?
quiz.a: v_out would need 2 V + 2 mA × 8 kΩ = 18 V, above the 12 V rail. The op-amp saturates, the drop across R falls below 2 V, and the current drops below 2 mA.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real current sources are sold as ICs with compliance range and thermal protection built in, and laser diode drivers add a monitor photodiode that closes a second loop around the set current. Industrial 4–20 mA transmitters pair a Howland-style pump with galvanic isolation, so a fault on the loop cannot reach the sensor. Transimpedance amplifiers set the noise floor of fibre-optic receivers, CT scanners and DNA sequencers, where most of the design work is the C_f compensation and the op-amp current noise. Search for the improved Howland current pump, transimpedance amplifier compensation, and the compliance voltage of a current source to go further.
